current_episode.title: Construction Tech Sales Explained with Gustavo de Bardeci

guest.bio_context: Gustavo de Bardeci, originally from Argentina, has spent 11 years in Australia working across the full project lifecycle — construction, operations, and design. He began his software career at Oracle and IBM, serving verticals such as financial services, utilities, and telecommunications in Latin America before relocating to Australia. His entry into construction technology came through Equinix, after which he worked at Aconex and NBS (National Building Specification) in the UK, before joining Revisto.

pending_qa.q: How deep does technical fluency need to go for a construction tech salesperson to be effective?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci argues that a salesperson does not need to be a BIM manager, but must know enough to ask intelligent questions and speak the language — models, drawings, issues, coordination, certifications, LODs. He describes this as 'technical fluency giving you permission to have a strategic conversation,' and stresses the importance of knowing when to bring in pre-sales or customer success teams for deeper technical discussions.

pending_qa.q: How does career progression work in construction tech sales, from individual contributor to leadership?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci explains that early-stage progression in sales is measured by activity — pipeline and closed deals. Over time, the bar shifts to understanding the market, building trusted relationships, influencing internal teams, and creating non-obvious opportunities. In the construction technology industry specifically, he emphasizes that the best progression is built through networking and reputation, not just title advancement.

pending_qa.q: What are the risks of short-term incentive structures in construction technology sales?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci warns that short-term incentive structures can push sales reps to oversell, overpromise, or push customers into discount clauses that kill retention and poison the customer relationship. In a long-term industry like construction, he argues that damaging a customer relationship to win a deal ultimately destroys a salesperson's reputation, which is their primary commercial asset.

pending_qa.q: How can you tell the difference between a salesperson who hits quota and one who builds a lasting reputation in construction tech?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci says the real measure is whether people call you when they change companies. Anyone can hit quota once, but those who build reputations are called upon across career moves. He frames it as a distinction between quota — which resets every year — and reputation — which compounds over an entire career.

pending_qa.q: What is the biggest misconception about salespeople in the construction technology industry?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci identifies the biggest misconception as the belief that salespeople are only there to negotiate price or push a contract. In reality, a good salesperson helps the customer frame the problem, understand the options, and avoid bad-fit solutions. He also notes that a healthy vendor relationship should involve some constructive challenge, not just agreement with everything the customer asks.

pending_qa.q: What separates a great construction software product from one that becomes noise in the market, according to a sales professional?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci states that adoption is the ultimate measure of a great construction product. The best products reduce friction across all roles — BIM managers, project managers, site teams, consultants, and owners — not just for the technical champion. He also points to ease of use as a critical differentiator, arguing that many construction software platforms are still designed primarily for technical users and fail the less tech-savvy daily users, which is where adoption breaks.

pending_qa.q: How important is the feedback loop between sales teams and product teams in construction technology companies?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci considers the sales-to-product feedback loop very important, but only when it is structured. He argues that unstructured feedback becomes noise, and that the best feedback loops separate one-off complaints from repeated patterns so the product team can act on what truly matters. He recommends involving customer success teams and industry consultants to collect and translate feedback to development teams.

pending_qa.q: Is AI genuinely changing how construction tech sales teams operate, or is it mostly theoretical?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci acknowledges that AI is genuinely changing parts of the sales workflow — particularly research, account planning, summarizing information, writing drafts, and preparing conversations. However, he does not believe AI replaces the human element of construction sales; if anything, it makes the human part more important, because everyone will have access to similar information and the differentiator will be who can build trust and understand customer context.

pending_qa.q: How have customer conversations about AI in construction technology shifted over the past year or two?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci observes that a year ago, AI conversations with customers were broad and theoretical. Today, customers are asking more practical questions — how AI will improve workflows, reduce admin, support decisions, or help teams manage project information. He notes that customers are less impressed by the word 'AI' and more interested in whether it solves something real.

pending_qa.q: Which human skills are becoming more important versus commoditized in construction tech sales as AI advances?
pending_qa.r: Gustavo de Bardeci identifies judgment, trust-building, curiosity, commercial empathy, and the ability to simplify complexity as the skills becoming more important in an AI-augmented sales environment. He considers outreach, research, follow-ups, and surface-level product information as already commoditized by AI tools — tasks that are largely automated and no longer a meaningful differentiator.
